body: List things to do, schedule on a calendar, and then check off each task as it is completed.
Brainstorm tasks to be done and then group items according to categories; nice vs. necessary or urgent vs. can wait.
Estimate or “guess–timate” the time required to complete a task and then record the actual time to complete it.
Develop a master semester schedule that includes exams and deadlines. Go to office hours if you might need help.
Prepare materials and place in a backpack or tote before you go to bed. This saves time and reduces hassle.
Plan your telephone contacts with friends and family. Schedule a  NO  CALL period during study time.
Schedule hour–by–hour, course–by–course study time. Check off each topic as completed, smile, and enjoy a break.
Develop a routine that allows for study and leisure. You need rest time to enhance attention and maintain motivation.
Warm up with a 5–minute break as a study warm–up; do a few stretches, take some deep breaths, and have a healthy drink or snack.
Remember to schedule intense, but brief 40–minute study times between classes at non–distracting locations.
Identify your peak learning times; schedule study times when you are most alert and able to focus and memorize.
Don’t tackle routine tasks until after study. For example, alphabetizing references or filing articles.
Try out your schedule for at least one week. This provides a realistic picture of what you actually get done.
Evaluate your schedule. Ask, “Did I over– or underestimate the time required to study a course? Any conflicts?”
Review the effectiveness of your weekly schedule and continuously adjust in order to increase your study efficiency.
Identify the time conflicts that challenge the quantity or quality of your study time. Studying when alert and relaxed.
Consider a study warm–up by doing some easier tasks before attacking material that is more difficult.
Use separate, color–coded binders or folders for each course.
Create a computer–based filing system to store supplemental readings and resources.
Schedule a regular time each week to delete or archive emails, newsletters, and other communication.
Purchase Blue Books or exam materials at the beginning of the semester to prevent problems on the day of the test.
Store pens pencils, staples, tape and other supplies in mugs or containers for easy access.
Designate a place to store credit card receipts in wallet or backpack.
Purchase a few memory sticks and back up work daily so that you don’t lose drafts of papers or projects.
Purchase an external drive to have a complete backup of reading assignments, papers, or projects.
Post due dates and instructions for each course’s assignments on a bulletin board or closet.
Clear the clutter on a desk or other workplace to reduce distractions and save time accessing materials.
Assemble or file papers and other materials at least once a week to increase control and efficiency.
Schedule one day a month to go to office hours or work with the instructor, teaching assistant or lab supervisor.
Check that work areas have ample and comfortable lighting. This increases your study energy and endurance.
Use helpful ideas from friends about the ways they organize their course materials, supplies and responsibilities.
Engage in a weekly, 5–minute self–dialogue to list the best ways you organized materials and space for better studying.
Prepare ways in which you will congratulate and reward yourself for staying organized and on target with your studies.
Post signs to remind you of the steps to follow when studying or writing a paper.
Keep a checklist of assignments and identify resources or materials to assemble prior to beginning your work.
Attend office hours to discuss the best ways to organize materials and approach the material for courses.
Keep a list or journal of lessons learned about organization of study materials and strategies. Review every 2 weeks.
Use online, print or audio resources to find tips about organization and storage of supplies, books and materials.
Use sketches and diagrams to specify the process and tasks needed to complete a long–term project.
Specify the plans for your day or for projects by talking into an audio recorder. If needed, make notes.
Use a file cabinet or milk crate to store materials for each course. Label or color code each for easy access.
Say directions aloud to keep you focused when following steps to complete a task or project.
Drink between 6 to 8 glasses of water daily to avoid symptoms of dehydration such as weakness, headaches and constipation.
Get at least 6 to 8 hours of sleep 4 to 5 days a week. Fatigue is the enemy of mental energy and alertness.
Take short naps of not more than 20 minutes in the late afternoon when energy and focus wane.
Avoid high intake of caffeine since it can trigger headaches, irritability, restlessness, and mild insomnia.
Avoid excessive sugar; an initial energy rush may soon be followed by tiredness, headaches and increases in hunger levels.
Incorporate some exercise within a total recreation plan. Exercise with a friend or join a running group.
Combine easy chores such as folding laundry with social chores such as talking on the telephone.
Balance physical and mental tasks; use a short study break to pack a lunch or open mail.
